stage_description: The juvenile or fledgling stage runs up to about 20% of a bird's expected lifespan. Now fully feathered, the young bird learns to fly, weans off formula onto solid food, and explores everything with intense curiosity. This is a highly formative window: the food preferences, social skills, and foraging habits set now will shape the rest of a life that may last anywhere from under a decade to half a century, depending on the species.
nutrition: Weaning is the moment to establish a healthy diet. Offer formulated pellets plus a variety of vegetables and leafy greens, with only limited seed and fruit, so the bird never becomes a fussy seed addict. Introduce many textures and colours while the bird is open to novelty, and provide fresh clean water at all times.
activity: Young birds are energetic, playful, and exploratory. Give plenty of supervised out-of-cage time, safe toys, and room to fly, plus gentle daily handling and exposure to household life to raise a confident, well-adjusted companion. Offer foraging toys now to build lifelong mental habits and head off boredom.
veterinary_check_frequency: Establish care with an avian (exotic) vet through a young-bird wellness exam. This visit may include a physical check, fecal testing, disease screening appropriate to the species, and a baseline weight. Discuss the diet transition and a lifelong preventive-care plan with the vet.
dental_care: The beak is now firm and keratinised and should be smooth, even, and properly aligned; birds have no teeth. Offer cuttlebone, a mineral block, and safe soft wood to help condition it. If you see any overgrowth or misalignment, have it assessed by an avian vet.
warning_signs: Refusing to wean or eat, losing weight, staying fluffed up, sitting on the cage floor, failing to fledge, or early feather-plucking all warrant concern. Because birds hide illness, any lethargy or appetite loss in a young bird is urgent — call an avian vet promptly.
source_name: AAV Care for Senior Parrots & Lafeber Vet
disclaimer: This information is for educational purposes only and does not replace consultation with a veterinarian.
